title: Swanson v. Citibank, N.A. (2010)
summary: The discrimination allegations identified a plausible dispute about a home appraisal and lending decision; a separate fraud theory failed.

sections.Parties: Swanson, a Black homeowner, sued Citibank and participants in the appraisal process after being denied a home-equity loan.
sections.Material Facts: Swanson sought a loan and believed her home was worth substantially more than the appraisal obtained in the lending process. The low appraisal prevented the loan, while another appraisal later valued the home more highly. She alleged that race affected the appraisal and lending decision, identifying the actors, transaction, and timing. She also attempted to plead fraud.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed the complaint. The Seventh Circuit reinstated the discrimination claim while leaving the dismissal of the fraud claim in place.
sections.Issue: Did the discrimination allegations provide a plausible claim after Twombly and Iqbal?
sections.Holding: Yes as to discrimination. The complaint supplied enough information about the alleged discriminatory transaction to proceed.
sections.Reasoning: The majority treated plausibility as requiring an account that made sense, while separating that inquiry from deciding whether discrimination was more likely than competing explanations. The complaint told the defendants who allegedly discriminated, what transaction was affected, and when it occurred. A legitimate appraisal explanation could be explored later. The fraud theory presented a distinct problem concerning the alleged loss and was not saved merely because the discrimination claim survived.

learning.why: The discrimination allegations identified a plausible dispute about a home appraisal and lending decision; a separate fraud theory failed.

topics.cp-plausibility: The majority found an intelligible who-what-when discrimination account plausible.
topics.cp-pleading-proof: The plaintiff did not need to eliminate every innocent appraisal explanation at filing.

learning.separateOpinions: Judge Posner dissented, emphasizing alternative explanations for the appraisal and the weakness of the inference of discrimination. The disagreement is useful for understanding how judges apply plausibility to the same factual narrative.
